speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley) moved:
subtopic: NORTHERN AND ISOLATED AREAS TAX ALLOWANCE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the discrepancies in the Northern and Isolated Areas Tax Allowance should be cleared up and the tax benefits continued.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in the House to speak to a motion sponsored by me that has been chosen for debate today.
The motion first presented some time ago reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the discrepancies in the Northern and Isolated Areas Tax Allowance should be cleared up and the tax benefits continued.
I have reviewed some of the previous debates on this issue. It is interesting to note that this may be the first real debate this House has had on this issue, certainly since changes were made to the program by the government in late 1990.
Before proceeding I want to thank a couple of my colleagues who have been helpful in our northern caucus in doing research and following this issue very closely.
The member for Churchill has done much of the work for our caucus on this issue. I thank him and his staff for their assistance. As well, the member for Skeena, whose seat adjoins mine to the west, has had much experience on this particular issue and has also provided valuable information. As well, my colleagues from Prince Albert-Churchill River and The Battlefords-Meadow Lake have participated in our caucus discussions. This is a very important issue to our constituents.
I thank them and others who have expressed their ongoing concern over this issue. I look forward to the debate and discussion today.
.(1115)
Canada is a northern country. Many of us now recognize that with the subtle change in our description of Canada as being from sea to sea to sea.
We now recognize that a large part of our country exists beyond the 49th parallel and our close relationship to the United States. Many of us who represent constituencies like mine also have communities that are remote even from the major centres in our own ridings. In my area, for example, communities like Fort St. James, Granisle and Valemount come to mind.
The important point to make is that these communities are just as much a part of Canada as are the cities we see most often on television and in the news. Our communities may not be the setting for programs like Street Legal and the like but they are part of what makes our country.
In fact many have argued that the wealth of Canada has been largely created by these remote areas. One just has to look at the forest industry for example. Over 300 communities in Canada depend on the forest industry for survival. Many communities live or die by the mining or fishing industry and their success or failure. It is the financial return to those businesses and the tax revenues to government that have enabled us to have many of the services we have today.
However, inherent in much of the way the system has evolved is that it is not fair in the way many of these communities are treated by the tax system and generally

March 15, 1993

speaking, by the lack of services and programs that government provides.
It is my view that the northern and isolated areas tax benefit program helped many of these communities and the rationale for reinstating the program in those areas that this government cut it from is still relevant today.
In a report prepared by the Library of Parliament a number of reasons were given as to why such a program was needed. The higher cost of living is mentioned, as is the lack of services that do not exist in many large centres or are taken for granted in many communities. It also notes that the northern tax benefit helps offset the higher tax burden on those who receive higher wages for just living and working in a community like this.
As a country, if we are to develop and gain from our resources we must be able to attract the people to those areas to help extract those resources and of course to hopefully add value to those raw resources. A benefit program helps with that. The development of these resources and these communities clearly helps all the people of our country.
I want to make the point as well that while my interest is in those areas which might normally be defined as northern, the original program was also for isolated areas. Living in certain parts of the Kootenays in British Columbia or parts of New Brunswick or Saskatchewan is just as remote as living in a northern community.
It is my view that not only should the program be reinstated, it should also be returned to those areas deemed remote that might have been eligible before. I will return to that point later.
Under the original program which came into effect in 1987 all individuals residing for at least six consecutive months in qualifying communities received a deduction of up to $450 per month. The key object at that time according to the Minister of Finance in a May 1990 response to a petition I tabled in the House was to "encourage workers to move to and settle in northern and isolated areas where recruitment is difficult".
The administration of the program was clearly a problem at the start. Members who have had experience with the system can cite many of them. Most of the problems resulted from boundary disputes-a point I will discuss later as well-in determining which communities were eligible.
As well, it would seem that the department, in this case National Revenue, certainly was not prepared for the administration of the program. Just to use one example in my riding, McBride which is east of Prince George was confused with McBride Lake which is south of Houston and a four hour drive from Prince George.
I am sure other members dealt with many similar problems my office had. Those of us who represent these northern communities, ourselves and certainly our staffs, have become somewhat expert in having to deal with the particular program and some of the discrepancies in it.
The problems were immense. In April 1988 the task force on tax benefits for northern and isolated areas was established to look at these problems. After public hearings were held throughout many areas the report was presented to the Minister of Finance on October 27, 1989. The report's recommendations were not well received in many parts of the country. Even the current Minister of Forestry, the member for Prince George- Peace River, said in the November 17,1989 Prince George Citizen that he was disappointed with the task force recommendations.
Among the problems with the task force was its initial instruction to produce a revenue neutral recommendation. This direction could only lead to a reduction in the program. I want to spend a bit of time on the next point because it goes to the crux of the problems the government has accepted and the alternative I wish to present.
The report's main recommendation was to reject the community-by-community approach. They argued that it was difficult to administer the program because of this and they developed a strict northern zone. Their argument was that the communities in the northern zone had the characteristics of being in the north. The question of being remote, that is a community in the Kootenays of British Columbia, was rejected out of hand.
Finally, after much prodding the government released its position in December 1990. The government's position was to accept the northern zone as recommended by the commission but to create an intermediate zone which reduces the program in that area to 50 per cent of the benefits by 1995, for example the community of Mackenzie which is not in my riding but north of Prince George. Communities outside the new area that were previously
March 15, 1993

eligible would see their benefits reduced by a third each year to the point where this year, tax year 1993, two-thirds of the benefit will be available. Then in tax year 1994 the last third will be provided. In 1995 the benefit would disappear completely.
I am calling for a return of the program to its original concept, including a return of full benefits and the inclusion of remote areas. I cannot see why we could not start with a new program of phasing in the new areas starting in tax year 1995 where we would start building the program back with two-thirds of the benefit being available again. This would mean that in 1996 the full benefit would be returned. Those communities which will only be receiving 50 per cent of the benefit in 1995-for example, Dawson Creek in northern British Columbia-could be returned immediately in my view to full benefits in the tax year 1994.
The main reason for the commission and the government to reject the program was that the community-bycommunity approach was too hard to administer; it was confusing and created too many discrepancies. It is my view that time has proven the government and the commission wrong on this point.
There is no doubt that the original program had many problems, as does the current one though on a much reduced scale. My research indicates that the problems on the whole have been resolved. For example, the Auditor General who had a team of auditors working on this program in the department removed them saying that the problems had largely been resolved, at least to the point where he no longer felt a need to have a specific monitoring of the department's administration of the program.
I have also discussed the problems with accountants in my riding who say that the number of problems has gone down dramatically. One firm reports that Revenue Canada reviewed 20 per cent to 30 per cent of northern tax benefit claims when the program started. This accountant now says that it is down to at most some 2 per cent. In other words, as soon as the government figured out how to run the program, it cancelled it. Unfortunately the government is not listening to people in those areas that want to see a return to the program.

In the December 21, 1990 Prince George Citizen the mayor of Mackenzie, British Columbia, just north of Prince George, a community in the phase-out area, hoped that there was "still an opportunity to talk to the government". Unfortunately that opportunity has come and gone. In an August 14,1992 letter to me the Minister of Finance said that the government "was not contemplating any change to the new program at this time".
It is unfortunate the Conservatives will not listen to northern or remote communities to have the program reinstated. They may be taking their cue from the Reform Party which apparently wants to axe this program completely. Northerners are obviously concerned about this lack of support from that particular party.
It is my view that a properly developed, well-known community-by-community system is the best approach to take. As we all know there are degrees of remoteness. A system well designed could be an ongoing measure of the level of services to a community. The more in improved services the less the benefit might be. It forces governments at all levels to be aware of the needs of remote communities, be it airport expansion or the provision of medical services.
Collective agreements already recognize the needs of employees who live in remote areas. For example, the isolated post directive is part of the collective agreement between the federal government and its employees. While these collective agreements recognize the needs of employees it is time the government did as well.
According to the Library of Parliament research paper on this issue, some 296,000 Canadians claimed the northern residence deduction. The "cost" to the government was thought to be around $305 million. That is a fraction of the defence department's $5.5 billion helicopter acquisition program and is a program that clearly would extend all across the country.
This program was a valuable one. It was well received by the public and once in place for some time the government departments charged with administering it were able to run it properly. In other words, it is a program worth keeping.

New Democrats have recently released a jobs paper that outlines our economic alternatives to this government and most important it clearly lays out our alternative in the tax field, something we have not heard from other parties. The measure alone on the GST would put at least another $600 a year in the pockets of each Canadian, not just northerners.
I welcome the comments from other members and hope that they will consider supporting this motion and allowing northerners the fairness we deserve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to share with hon. members my views on motion M-376, which suggests that the alleged discrepancies in the northern and isolated areas tax allowance should be cleared up and the tax benefits continued.
First of all, I would like to give you a brief history of these tax benefits for residents in northern and isolated areas. In the late 1970s a routine audit by Revenue Canada, Taxation revealed that many employees in northern and isolated areas received assistance from their employers for housing and travel. The value of this assistance was not always reported on information slips, even though it clearly constituted a tax benefit under the Income Tax Act. A proposal by Revenue Canada to adjust the tax returns of affected individuals generated great concern. In order to study the issues, the government announced a moratorium on taxation of these benefits.
This moratorium was implemented by means of a remission order. From 1978 to 1986 certain employer-provided travel and housing benefits for workers in eligible isolated areas were exempted from income tax. In his budget of November 12, 1981 the Minister of Finance announced his intention to limit the application of the remission order to employees who had participated in benefit plans established on or before that date. On December 2, 1982, plans for phasing in the taxation of these benefits and rules for their evaluation were announced. Evaluation rules were set up in a second
remission order. However, the proposal to phase in taxation of these benefits was subsequently rescinded.
The government continued to study the issue. Concerns were expressed at meetings held in Northern Canada with local residents and groups representing employees, entrepreneurs, native people and others.
Two themes were a constant in these discussions. First, employers reported difficulties in attracting and retaining employees. Second, certain aspects of the remission orders were felt to be unfair because they benefited only workers receiving housing and travel assistance from their employers, and only employees covered by arrangements made prior to November 13,1981 were entitled to a full exemption.
Acknowledging the inequities of the remission order system the Minister of Finance proposed in his budget of February 26, 1986 that the tax benefit should apply to all residents of qualifying areas. These areas were identified community by community, on the basis of factors such as distance from an urban centre, condition of roads and latitude. According to this approach, which was applied from 1987 to 1991, all employer-provided benefits became taxable but certain tax deductions became available to all residents of qualifying areas. A transitional deduction was granted to residents in areas that were previously covered by remission orders but no longer qualified for the tax deduction.
Unfortunately, determining qualifying areas on a community-by-community basis did not prove as effective as the government had hoped. Although many of the discrepancies referred to in the hon. member's motion were eliminated the government continued to receive many representations stating that the northern tax benefits system remained unfair, mainly because some communities located near qualifying communities were not eligible.
On December 10, 1987 the Minister of Finance announced his intention to establish a task force to study the appropriateness of changing the eligibility criteria for determining the Northern and Isolated Areas Tax Allowance. The task force was instrumental in moving this debate forward, suggesting in its report published in 1989 that a zone system should replace community-based
March 15, 1993

determination of qualifying areas, in determining eligibility for benefits available to residents of northern and isolated areas.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, and as some members of this Elouse may be aware as well, a zone system was introduced in 1991. The zones did not cover all communities previously covered by the remission order system or community-based determination of qualifying areas. However, residents of these communities were and still are receiving benefits on a transitional basis. These transitional benefits will be phased out gradually by 1994, by which time we will have eliminated many of the inequities of the previous systems. The new zone system has already simplified the process considerably and is a more effective way of assisting residents of northern and isolated areas.
Considering these developments, I think all hon. members will agree that previous measures to determine eligibility for the Northern and Isolated Areas 'lax Allowance have proved unfair and ineffective. Perhaps it would be easier to understand the problems that existed under the old system and the kind of discrepancies involved if I were to describe a typical case.
Consider the person who lives just outside the perimeter of a qualifying community. He works for the same employer, goes to the same grocery store, has the same family doctor and has access to the same local school as another person who lives within the perimeter of the qualifying community.
Under the old community-based system for determining qualifying areas one person was eligible for tax benefits while the other was not. To make matters worse, although the person outside the perimeter of this community was actually living in greater isolation he was nevertheless not eligible for these benefits. It has been said that the community-by-community method for determining qualifying areas was inherently unfair because it created border problems between adjacent communities that were treated differently for income tax purposes.
Mr. Speaker, let me tell you now why I believe that the present system of zones is a better solution and probably
Private Members' Business
the best solution for determining eligibility for these benefits.
In its report of October 27, 1989, the task force on tax benefits for northern and isolated areas proposed creating only one northern area in which residents have major problems and are isolated. The task force recommended that only residents of the northern area continue to receive tax benefits and that the transition period for communities losing benefits not exceed one year.
The task force stated just as clearly that the then-current method of determining prescribed zones community by community could not be maintained. The government therefore had to choose one of two alternatives: either a modified method of determining prescribed zones community by community, like the one that existed before, or a zone system. Since experience had shown that a system of determining prescribed zones community by community was untenable, the government accepted the task force's proposal to establish a zone system.
The present system of zones is based on recommendations from the task force and many other presentations received throughout the country. Areas eligible for the deductions given to northerners, which are areas in the north and in the intermediate zone, were defined using two classification systems developed by the task force.
The northern area classification system included mainly environmental factors like the severity of the climate, the growing season, the heating season, plant cover and permafrost. The classification system for isolated regions put more emphasis on community characteristics such as population and distance from urban centres. This is an effective and objective way of determining eligibility for the deductions given to northerners.
According to this method, northerners are eligible for full benefits, while residents of the intermediate zone are eligible for half the benefits. Furthermore, as I already said, transitional provisions were established. Residents of communities that are no longer eligible under the zone system will receive two-thirds of the benefits in 1993 and one-third in 1994. Only after that date will benefits be fully eliminated.
No perfect system exists. Whatever solution we decide on to determine eligibility for the northern benefit some people will still believe that they should be included if we want the system to be fair.

March 15, 1993
Private Members' Business
Nevertheless, extending the benefits further south would reduce the relative advantages for those who are really isolated. I believe that our present system is the best. It is based on the objective opinions we received from an independent task force. It gives a temporary break to those who are no longer eligible for benefits or those whose benefits will be reduced. At the end of the transition period, the new system will have eliminated many, if not all, of the inequities in the former system.

The next issue is the one dealing with isolation. Isolation can be easily broken down into certain categories: one, the availability of basic services in a community; two, the availability of basic goods in a community; three, where goods are regularly available, their costs including transportation and transportation taxes; and four, where goods and services are not available, the availability and cost of transportation to and from the closest service centre.
In my mind it is easy to make a decision as a government as to whether people meet certain criteria based on living in northern Ontario and establishing criteria to deal with isolation. For example, in some communities in northern Ontario there are no publicly funded elementary schools. In some communities there are no publicly funded high schools. In some communities there are no publicly funded medical facilities. In some communities there are no banks or other financial institutions, no post offices or no telephone service.
Those unique needs require some sort of northern tax allowance benefit. If they can easily be put into a criteria, then based on that criteria we could decide what level of benefits would be given. It could then be phased in depending on where communities would fall in terms of the kinds of services and products they would want to offer.
For example, let us talk about transportation. Some communities are only accessible by air. Communities in northern Ontario that are only accessible by air should get 100 per cent of the northern tax allowance because it makes obvious sense that if a community is so isolated that it has no road, no railway, no bus, and only possibly air access, then more than likely it does not have very good medical facilities and those other kinds of situations that we are talking about.
To identify isolated areas we could also use the costs of goods that come to people in that community. We could easily use the CPI standard. Let me give an example of how we could do that. Lac la Croix is a community that was phased out under the new northern residence deduction system that the minister implemented in

1990-91. Lac la Croix is being phased out and should not be simply for the reason that it is only accessible by air. So it should get 100 per cent of the NRD. Ignace, which is a community in northern Ontario that is on the Trans-Canada Highway, only has bus service so it should be allowed, and this is only a suggestion of course so we can fool around with the numbers, to get 25 per cent based on the fact that it only has bus service.
Then there is the CPI which is much higher than in southern Ontario. It would give them about another 20 percentage points so a community like Ignace which was completely phased out should get roughly 45 per cent of the tax benefits under the northern tax allowance. Savant Lake has no public transportation, no banks, and no high schools so based on the criteria that I have outlined it would get 110 points, which is over 100 so it would get 100 per cent of the northern tax allowance.
That is how the system should have been put in place to deal with the isolation of northern Canadians. It should not have suggested that now we will arbitrarily create a zone somewhere in northern Ontario, northern B.C. or northern Alberta. In effect, that pits one northerner against another.
The whole objective was to give benefits to people who would not be able to access the services that we just take for granted in urban centres in this country.
I suggest to the government that if it had listened to the suggestions that were made by northerners and by members of Parliament on this side of the House then it would have implemented a system that was much more acceptable to all of us and which would have met the criteria it established when it first tried to implement this new system. That criteria was to stimulate economic development and growth, entice people from southern portions of our country to come to northern Canada to work, and to give them those benefits which would reduce the cost of living for those northerners.
I appreciate the short period of time I was given to outline a much more acceptable way of giving northerners the northern tax allowance.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today on my party's motion to speak about a new vision for Canada. As the motion we put before the House
March 15, 1993

outlines, this vision is based on an economic recovery program that must endorse a full employment strategy. We have seen the results of the old vision. We want to present a new vision.
The results of the old vision are quite clear: a huge debt, started by the Liberals and doubled by the Conservative Party, off-loaded onto the provinces and territories; over 1.5 million Canadians officially unemployed and thousands more having left the work force after giving up hope completely; and a 17 per cent unemployment rate in the youth of our country, and this is of particular concern when the youth cannot see a future for themselves, and four million Canadians living in poverty. We have seen the results of the old vision.
The Conservatives can select a new leader. They can put a new face on old policies but they remain old policies and they remain failed policies. More than a new face, Canada requires a new direction.
My party has put forward a detailed jobs plan which presents that new direction, which proposes a fundamental reorientation of economic policy away from the failed trickle-down approach to a policy founded on a full employment strategy. We have to destroy the myth that the economic policy which puts 1.5 million Canadians out of work is good economic policy. We have to destroy the myth that words such as a jobless recovery even mean anything. We need an economy that puts people first. We have to destroy the myth that the answer to our problems is to attack the unemployed.
The answer is not to attack the unemployed but to attack unemployment. A full employment strategy allows us to do just that.
What is a full employment strategy? It means that every economic policy would be reoriented so that every government action affecting the economy would ask the question, will this protect jobs, will this create jobs? This includes training policies and education policies. All of the actions the government would take would be oriented to ensuring that Canadians are working.
The jobs plan that we put forward would create 1.6 million new jobs over the length of the next Parliament. That is 500,000 more jobs than if Canada continued under the current policies. At the same time our plan

would lower the deficit, would bring down inflation and hold the line on taxes for middle-income Canadians.

We succeed because we recognize that the government has a constructive role to play in the economy. The other parties do not admit that.
The economies that came out of the 1980s in good shape are those where the governments played a constructive role in co-operation with business and labour. If I may, I would like to briefly highlight a few of the initiatives that we propose in this new vision.

First there is the physical infrastructure. Canadian businesses need good transportation systems. They need modern telecommunications systems and healthy communities. What they have is an infrastructure that has been deteriorating for 20 years through negligence.
We have a choice: either invest now or wait and pay 10 times as much. In our plan, we have chosen the most sensible approach, a national infrastructure program that will take us into the 21st century and create 130,000 jobs.
What the government has neglected in recent years is the social infrastructure-social programs, education and the health system-which is the basis of a strong, sound economy. We must rejuvenate our social infrastructure and fill the gaps in it, the biggest one being the lack of a national child care program.
A national child care program would give our children a sound pre-school education and enable parents to devote themselves to their own training and to finding work. This is now impossible, especially for single mothers.
Our action plan proposes a national child care program that would double the number of places in Canada in five years and create 70,000 jobs.

A third issue in our plan addresses the need to get more capital into the hands of small and medium-sized businesses. It is these businesses that create 75 per cent to 80 per cent of employment in Canada. It is a particularly important issue, I might add, for those entrepreneurs who live outside major cities and in less populated regions.
We see an important role for government here in helping to establish pools of capital that will invest in innovative Canadian-owned companies that create jobs here at home. Our plan presents a national investment fund that has a potential to create 200,000 new Canadian jobs.
Another important initiative we propose is a fair tax system, an important part of providing revenues and also providing a climate of fairness in our country. A part of that is the elimination of the GST. By the way, I am pleased to note that this past weekend Australia learned from our experience and elected a Labour government opposed to the GST.
In Canada, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business has estimated that the GST costs businesses in this country about $10 billion to collect and has cost the country 100,000 to 200,000 jobs.
Of course, any responsible party advocating the elimination of the GST has to spell out exactly how it would plan to replace revenues. We do that in the jobs plan. I want to say that these options are reasonable and indeed, by eliminating the GST, maintain a low rate of inflation, something that has not happened with the continuation of the current economic policies.
Of course, the Liberals said that they too would eliminate the GST, but they do not tell us how. They talk about another kind of consumption tax, maybe a tax on everything, maybe a tax on food. If it looks like a duck and walks like a duck, it must be a duck. We are saying that it is in the interest of the country and the economic interest to eliminate the GST. We are serious about it and we provide the alternatives.
The final policy I want to mention today is trade. Our party's policy is very clear. We believe that the Canada-

U.S. trade deal must be abrogated and that NAFTA must not proceed.
Why is that so crucial? It is crucial simply because Canada cannot pursue a new vision and cannot pursue the kind of new economy that we are talking about if we are bound by trade deals that entrench the old vision and the old way of doing things: trade deals which prevent the government from playing a positive role in the economy and which take away from Canadians the instruments of regional development, resource development, value-adding and strategic investment.
Let us be clear about what these trade deals represent. They represent taking power away from elected, accountable people's democratic governments and transferring it to unaccountable, unelected multinational corporations. This is not in the interest of Canada nor, I might add, of any other country.
We believe that if we are to ensure the long-term viability of Canada as a great trading nation, we must replace the so-called free trade agreements with a fair trade strategy based on sectoral agreements, improved multilateral arrangements and aggressive trade diversification to areas like the Pacific Rim.

These are the highlights of our action plan to create jobs and revive our economy. I did not mention all the initiatives in this plan for research and development, for example, to increase opportunities for training, to create opportunities for our young people, to develop our rural communities and those that depend on natural resources.
How do we create 1.6 million jobs while reducing the deficit and controlling inflation, without increasing taxes for our families? The answer is found in my party's innovative approach to the economy.

There are two deficits in this country, both of which we take seriously. There is the fiscal deficit, which is very real and which we must all be concerned about. There is also the human deficit, the energy, talent and potential we are losing because so many people live in poverty, are unemployed or are in part-time, short-term jobs.
The approach taken by the Conservatives and the Liberals is that the only way to improve the fiscal deficit is to worsen the human deficit. In fact, through that approach they have worsened both.
Our approach is that the only way to improve the fiscal deficit situation is to work to eliminate the human deficit. Our plan will generate 1.6 million new jobs,
500.000	more than under current policies. Think of
500.000	additional workers able to pay taxes. Think of
500.000	fewer Canadians dependent on government support. Think of the resulting reduction in the deficit and the debt.
It has been estimated that the gap between Canada's actual economic output and its potential output is $70 billion. Not only does that represent an economic deficit, a fiscal deficit, but it clearly represents the human deficit.
Getting Canadians back working again will fill that gap. Filling that gap will contribute to substantial deficit and debt reduction. The reality is we have a choice in this country: We can carry on with the slash and bum or we can start to plant and grow.
That is our plan. Perhaps because the logic has not been fully grasped by some of our colleagues in the other two parties our plan has been opposed by the two old parties. I invite a debate. I invite the Conservatives and the Liberals to produce their own alternatives.
Politics in this country has changed. Canadians have come to expect an open and thorough discussion of issues. They want and deserve to know where political parties stand before an election, not after.
Canadians deserve to be listened to. Canadians deserve to be involved. Only in that way can we determine Canada's economic future. Only in that way can we restore Canadians' confidence in the political process. Only in that way can we restore optimism and hope to the people whom we are here to serve.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to my hon. friend, the leader of the New Democratic Party, who is now fleeing the House because she does not want to hear what the Conservatives have to say.
I find the New Democratic Party's policies rather fascinating. I have spent time reading its economic document. Let us get this straight. The NDP proposes cancelling the free trade agreement. That is the first thing it is going to do, cancel the free trade agreement. In doing that, it is obviously going to bring back all the tariffs on the products that we ship into the United States, primarily further manufactured goods-there

March 15, 1993
Supply
were no tariffs on the raw materials and so on-where we have made the most progress in the free trade agreement. It is going to bring the free trade agreement back and put all those tariffs back up again.
Not only are the NDP putting tariffs on Canadian goods going into the United States, it will be putting tariffs on American goods coming into Canada which will jack up the price of the goods that we consume in this country. Therefore inflation is going to increase. It does not talk about that.
As a matter of fact, in its economic program it did brag about a company that did a study on it but did not take into consideration what cancellation of the free trade agreement would do to the economy of this country. It was not taken into consideration.
The next thing the NDP is going to do is stop the negotiations on NAFTA, just stop them. Never mind that almost everything Mexico ships into Canada now is duty free. The problem is getting our further manufactured goods into Mexico with high tariffs on them, some of them up to 25 per cent.
My friend from Broadview-Greenwood talked about telecommunications. I can tell the House that telecommunications is one area where we have great expertise and are doing extremely well, as well as in the environmental end of things. There are companies in Canada producing wonderful environmental equipment which is now being exported world-wide and in which Mexico has a great interest. Reducing the tariffs on these particular items will be beneficial to this country.
The NDP is going to cancel the North American free trade agreement. Then it is going to cancel the goods and services tax. I am the first to admit that the goods and services tax was probably not one of the most popular policies that any government in the last half century has brought in. However, I want it made very clear that there were innumerable studies, two royal commissions and joint committees of the Senate and the House of Commons. House of Commons committees over the last 40 years have recommended that Canada get out of the manufacturers' sales tax, which was at 13.5 per cent, and get into a form of consumption tax.
In our first mandate between 1984 and 1988 broad discussion took place across this country on the type of value-added tax we might have. A decision was taken by
this government and in the 1988 election campaign one of the planks in our platform was the goods and services tax. Nobody can deny that. It was there. It was debated. I remember the Minister of Finance at the time made two commitments during the campaign, no tax on food, on basic groceries, and no tax greater than there was on housing under the manufacturers' sales tax.
I remember very clearly that that was debated in 1988. It was not a surprise. It was part of the tax reform program and it was coming. The opposition can talk about free trade getting us elected, not the goods and services tax. That does not matter. We got elected, we formed the government and that was part of the plank of the platform. It was brought in.
I think manufacturers and exporters will tell you that one of the reasons we are more competitive in the international marketplace today is because of the goods and services tax, absolutely. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association will tell you that and the exporters will tell you that. We are not taxing our Canadian manufactured goods more than we are our imports as we did under the old system. We are not doing that any more. The NDP is going to cancel that.
It is $15 billion, $16 billion, $17 billion in income for the government. How is the NDP going to make it up? It has listed a number of things as to how it is to make it up, but at the same time it is going to bring in a national child care program costing about $6 billion. It is going to bring in a make-work project. It does not have a price tag on it, but it is a very expensive one. As is pointed out in its paper in the near term it is going to have to borrow. But it also says that in the near term it is going to get interest rates down.
When governments go out to borrow and increase their deficits, interest rates will follow because there will be insecurity throughout the financial markets where they must go to borrow and they will have to pay a premium to borrow money which will crank up the interest rates and start this old cycle of inflation up again.
The piece of work that the New Democratic Party has come out with is Alice in Wonderland. Grimm could not write a better fairy tale. There is no realism in it at all. It sounds beautiful and it looks beautiful on paper but if the NDP does everything that it says it is going to do in this paper then we are in for one terrible financial
March 15, 1993

situation. There is no question about that. We would be in more financial problems that you can imagine.
I want to state something that is rather interesting. I am fortunate enough to sit around the table with the Minister of Finance and the other finance ministers of this country. In the last while the New Democratic finance ministers are all of a sudden singing a little different tune than they did when they were campaigning or when they were in office for the first year or two. All of a sudden reality struck. Lo and behold they are talking about cost cutting. They are talking about deficit reduction. They are talking about reducing their borrowing requirements. Surprise, surprise. All of a sudden reality has hit.
I and a number of my colleagues will be speaking about some of the initiatives that were brought out in detail by the New Democratic Party. What I would like to do for a few moments is take a look at some of the things that are affecting Canada today and why the government has to move in the way it has been moving and I assume will continue to move.
There is a quickly moving global economy out there. The new world order for Canada's main street is Rome to Rangoon. It is not just Halifax or St. John's, Newfoundland, to Vancouver or even just down to New York, Chicago or Atlanta.
This is an environment where brainpower, technology and competitive muscle, not just our natural resources, are keys to our economic prosperity. This is a context where we transmit knowledge and money at the speed of light to and from every corner of the world.
These forces have led to a world of greater interdependence and competition than ever before in history. It is having a tremendous impact everywhere, but especially for Canada. In a world that is trading more Canada has become one of the great world traders. There are 114 separate countries whose yearly trade with Canada exceeds $10 million. Exports account for about 30 per cent of our economy, millions of jobs. Of the world's seven largest economies, only Germany depends more on trade than Canada.
Much of our exports are natural resources such as paper products, ores and fuels. These are commodities

marked by low prices that offer few new job opportunities. The direction Canada must now pursue is toward the knowledge-based higher margin products that can deliver good products and good jobs, and it is happening. We have had success stories that are second to none, such as large firms like Loblaws in food products and Spar in aerospace technology.
Canadian firms are finding niches around the world. I look at my friend from London, Labatt's, which bought Italy's Moretti SPA which now brews Italy's third largest selling brand of beer and smaller firms such as Montreal's Soft Image Inc. whose technology has cornered 70 per cent of the Italian market for 3-D computer software. There are stories after stories after stories, which I know my friend from Broadview-Greenwood agrees with, of successes of Canadian entrepreneurship and expertise around the world.

What about your friend from Hamilton and
Stelco?

I will tell you what is going to happen to Stelco in Hamilton. Once it modernizes, streamlines and reorganizes it will become one of the best steel companies in the world and will be back on its feet doing extremely well. I predict that Dofasco will do the same, but it is experiencing the same problems that steel companies around the world are experiencing, which are reorganization and the reality of what is happening in the world today.
That is one of the things that I think all members of Parliament understand is going on in the world today. We see it time and time again.
You don't know what the problem is.

My friend from Hamilton West will have ample opportunity to debate today. I will be pleased to sit and listen to his side of the argument if he would just give me a chance to give my side of it. I would appreciate it.
At a time when these jobs are so important and so mobile, a nation's tax system must play a critical role in attracting or driving away business. We have met that

challenge by reforming our tax system. I talked about the goods and services tax but we also changed our business tax and the income tax system to make it fairer and more responsive to what is going on in the world today.
I notice that the New Democratic Party now wants to add a number of tax categories to income tax, and that is fine. It wants to go back and I understand that. The New Democratic Party wants to go back to the old ways. It wants to bring in the high tariff barriers again and the old tax systems again. It wants to go back.
We cannot go back any more. The New Democratic Party must understand and must learn that. As a result of the changes that we have brought about, Canada is now in the position of having veiy positive growth potential. There is not a think-tank around that is not saying that Canada is going to have the best growth in the OECD this year. The reason they are saying that is because interest rates are down and inflation is down. A lot of people do not understand the importance of getting inflation down.
Let me just talk about that. Inflation is a hidden tax, and I want people to look at it that way. Inflation is a hidden tax on young and old and on our ability to compete in the global marketplace. It eats up savings, making it harder for a young Canadian to buy a home or for parents to put aside money to help pay for their children's education. It costs workers jobs by pushing up wage demands and the costs of doing business, making it harder for us to export and leaving us more vulnerable to imports.
Inflation is no longer stealing Canadians' savings and killing jobs. Our average rate of inflation for 1992 was 1.5 per cent, the lowest in 30 years. It was also the lowest rate among the world's seven largest economies. Bringing down inflation has been a success that we can take to the bank. The simple fact is that lower inflation is the key to lower interest rates, and we are seeing results.
Low inflation has not only reduced interest rates but has also helped bring the growth of labour costs down sharply. This translates into Canadian companies being better able to compete at home and in the global marketplace.
The global economy has been struggling. Time after time we see these announcements of other countries with restructuring problems and lay-offs entering a
recessionaiy period such as we are now seeing in Germany and France.
As a result of that and because the economy's growth is slow the Minister of Finance introduced some help for the small business sector last year. The hon. leader of the New Democratic Party touched on the small business sector today and she is absolutely right. It is very important since between 1979 and 1990 it created some two million new full-time jobs, more than 80 per cent of all new employment. As a result of their importance, small business corporations enjoy a special deduction which holds the federal income tax rate to 12.8 per cent on the first $200,000 of business income. In the United States federal rates for small firms range from 15 per cent to 39 per cent over the same income range.
We have put in place a tax situation for small businesses to help them. As well, in the financial statement we helped them with their unemployment insurance employer premiums for jobs created in 1993. We have encouraged increased investment with the one-year 10 per cent investment tax credit for machinery and equipment which will apply to small businesses in farming, fishing, mining, oil and gas, manufacturing, construction and long-haul transportation.
We have also taken action to help small businesses secure financing. I could list the things we have done there but I can only say that time is running out and I cannot run through them all. I want to touch on a couple of other things.
The policies on housing have been very positive. There was the reduction of the required down payment from 10 per cent to 5 per cent, which 69,000 Canadian families took advantage of last year. I know my hon. friend from London was urging the government to do that, as were the real estate associations.
Then there were the RRSPs. We do not know exactly how much went into housing but we do know that
127,000	withdrawals were made in 1992, totalling $1.2 billion. We have to assume that a good portion of that amount went to housing.
Housing starts grew by 6.3 per cent last year and we are expecting a further 5.2 per cent growth this year. As a result of the affordability due to low inflation and the sharp decline in mortgage rates, the proportion of renters who can now afford a home has surged. For example, the proportion of renters in Toronto who can
March 15, 1993

afford to buy a home jumped nearly five times, from 7.3 per cent in January 1991 to 35 per cent by October of last year.
We have to continue our fight against overspending in government at all levels. The Canadian people are telling us in no uncertain terms that co-operation between all levels of government must intensify when it comes to tax matters and wisely spending the taxpayers' dollar.
That is probably the strongest message being received today from people from all parts of our economy. It is incumbent upon us to do that very thing. In co-operation with provincial and municipal governments we must get our act together, if I can use such a hackneyed expression, because that is what they are asking for.
That is what Canadians are encouraging us to do. We have provided the leadership in that area with the suggestions contained in the proposals in the Constitution which can be used as a basis for discussions between provincial governments and the federal government to assure that the taxpayers' dollar is being spent wisely or being saved wisely. We tend to forget that it all comes out of one person's pocket, the taxpayer, whether it is at the federal level, the provincial level or the municipal level.
I believe our policies are working. We are positioned to take advantage of economic growth this year. We will see a real gross domestic product increase of some 3.5 per cent, marking the seventh consecutive quarterly increase which is the largest since the second quarter of 1991. We must stay the course. If we deviate from this course then the financial markets will let us know in no uncertain terms and we will experience uncertainty once again.

The New Democratic Party says that we are playing politics. That statement was just made. On top of that, this government should not have rushed headlong into negotiating a North American free trade agreement when there was unfinished business. Mr. Speaker, for all its ambiguity it seems that the motion we are being asked to address today offers a simplistic and flawed prescription for the ailing Canadian economy. It seeks to turn the clock back in effect on eight years of Conservative rule.
It is true that the motion contains a rather woolly reference to a jobs plan, whatever that might mean in an era of federal and provincial fiscal crisis, and an infrastructure program. There is vague reference to a national child care program.
The real essence of the motion is profoundly reactionary. It holds out the deceptively simple idea that by attempting to reverse the course of Conservative policy over the last eight years, by abrogating the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, terminating our participation in the North American free trade agreement, renationalizing industries and reopening the fiscal sluices to the provinces, we can somehow return Canada to a golden age of full employment.
In one of the ironic twists of history the New Democratic Party, once one of Canada's great agents of reform, has become profoundly conservative, a party of resistance to change, a party yearning to return to the status quo ante.
Let me say first of all that we in the Official Opposition reject any such course of action or reaction for two principal reasons.
First, it is simply impossible to turn the clock back. Of course policies can be undone, legislation can be rolled back and international commitments can be terminated. That much is relatively easy, if costly, for a future Canadian government.
What cannot be reversed, however, are the forces of technological and global change. Microprocessors, fibre optics, telecommunications satellites, transnational corporations are the real factors, are the fundamental factors that are driving the transformation of the Canadian economy. It is not the FTA or the GST or any other policy acronym which the New Democratic Party may choose to target. These developments are ensuring that the Canadian economy will be pried open, not just to the United States, but to the world whether we like it or not.
To this extent policies such as the free trade agreement mark an accelerated reflection of changes that were already occurring world-wide.
The real question is what the Canadian government should offer Canadians to help them benefit from, and not be victimized by, these global changes. Canada cannot hide itself from these changes.
As we see from its motion today, the NDP would have us believe that the best response to globalization is to rebuild the walls around Canada and attempt to hold back the forces of world change. Such an approach would

March 15, 1993

simply reduce the ability of the Canadian economy to modernize and adapt to the emerging international market. Far from creating jobs and prosperity, such an approach would further erode the living standards and prospects of all Canadians.
The immutable fact is that globalization currently requires, and will continue to demand, important restructuring in industrial economies including that of Canada. This is regardless of which federal or provincial party is in power and the ideologies that it espouses. In particular, economic transformation, emphasizing product and process innovations, improved product quality, reduced costs, greater labour skills, more effective marketing and increased productivity and flexibility in the economy is now a prerequisite for Canadian competitiveness across all sectors, from resource industries to high technology.
Canada's future lies in global links and in securing access to the world's dynamic economies, not just the United States but with the Pacific rim and the increasingly integrated European Community.
The salient question is no longer whether we should limit ourselves to fortress Canada, as the NDP would have us do, but whether we can afford to limit ourselves to fortress North America.
The second and more important reason that we reject the approach implicitly advocated in part of this motion is that it misses the real implications of eight years of Conservative rule, irrespective of the government's rhetoric about the tough and politically costly decisions which it has taken on behalf of Canadians. The real story is not what the government has done over the past eight years to help prepare Canadians for globalization, but what it has failed to do on the debt, on economic restructuring, on reforming social programs, on investing in Canadians and so forth.
When future historians write of these eight years of Conservative government rule, it will be a story of years of delayed decisions, of uncertain and irresolute leadership and, most of all, of missed opportunities.
Of all the government's failures, the one that is most central to Canada's current economic malaise and the one that, significantly, today's NDP motion simply ignores is the inability to arrest, let alone reverse, this country's accelerating debt crisis. Underpinning the
current economic crisis is the fact that consumption in Canada has consistently outpaced savings and real economic growth.
The Conservative Party that came to power in 1984 promising debt reduction above everything else chose to attempt to solve the problem not through the restructuring and streamlining of government-spending reductions have in fact received only perfunctory treatment by this government-but through massive increases in taxation.
Under the Conservatives, profligate government spending and constantly increasing taxation, both at the federal and provincial levels, led in turn to the over-stimulation of an already stimulated Canadian economy. In order to take inflationary pressure out of the economy, the Bank of Canada raised interest rates. Higher interest rates led to higher debt service costs and yet more deficit spending. This, in turn, resulted in further stimulation of the economy and yet more inflation.
The result of these policy failures is today a net public debt amounting to more than $650 billion. Meanwhile, we are running a current account deficit of well over 4 per cent of our gross domestic product, which is by far the worst performance among OECD countries today.
A less obvious result of this prolonged period of over-consumption has been a growing foreign indebtedness and a weakening of Canada's economic base. Indeed Canada has rapidly become such a large offshore borrower that the level of foreign debt has risen to over $200 billion, not to mention an additional $100 billion in private debt.
What are the costs of all this to Canadians? Instead of undertaking the kind of investments needed to prepare for a globalized economy, we are faced with unacceptably high real interest rates-I say real interest rates-needed to attract offshore capital, a dated and declining infrastructure, growing deficits in skills, training and education, and of course a mounting foreign debt which will inevitably be paid back out of the future living standards of Canadians.
The challenge is obvious and fundamental. There is not a word in this NDP resolution about the need to resolve our fiscal imbalances and foreign indebtedness. By contrast, the Leader of the Opposition, the leader of

the Liberal Party of Canada, has been clear about the helped business and labour adapt to new opportunities tasks before the next government.	and to new competition.
Recently the Leader of the Opposition said that never before has Canada been so much a prisoner of foreign creditors. The Conservatives have borrowed too much abroad and they have borrowed too much in the short term. Canada has too many IOUs in the hands of foreigners. A Liberal government will aim at paying our way in the world. We must balance our international current account so that we can create jobs at home and not export them abroad.
The Conservative failure to restructure government over the last eight years has not just resulted in a mounting debt crisis and the high levels of unemployment that we have experienced recently. By refusing to confront the need for root and branch reform to the way government services are delivered in this country, the government has also refused to recognize the direct linkage between economic liberalization and the need for major domestic reform and adjustment.
During the prolonged debates about the merits or demerits of freer trade, whether it was about the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement or NAFTA or the pending but far more pervasive Uruguay round of the GATT, there has been singularly little discussion of adjustment assistance. The phrase has a boring or even bureaucratic ring about it, yet it is adjustment assistance in all its many forms that can make the inevitable dislocations engendered by freer trade more understandable and more palatable even to those who are adversely affected, as some always unfortunately will be. Instead today, unlike in past years, large numbers of Canadians are left bewildered by freer trade.
For more than four decades Canadians have been assured by their governments that as a people heavily dependent on exports for their prosperity improved access to foreign markets and the parallel opening of our own markets was unquestionably good for them. The successive freer trade rounds of the GATT, although perhaps invisible to many, did undeniably contribute massively to Canada's affluence. However, part of the reason the Kennedy or Tokyo rounds did so was that they were matched by a commensurate degree of adjustment assistance, which were government initiatives that
Following the precedents of the various GATT rounds, the Macdonald royal commission in recommending the negotiation of a free trade agreement with the United States urged repeatedly that any such agreement be matched with comprehensive adjustment assistance in the form of training and retraining, investment incentives, the elimination of interprovincial trade barriers and so forth.
The government did not do this despite promises that it would. It sought a free trade agreement with the United States but it did not devise, based on its own studies of the likely impact of free trade, those sectoral, regional or other assistance programs that would have helped to lessen the inevitable dislocation and assist Canadians to compete more effectively.
Instead of additional jobs many Canadians have seen unemployment. Tariff reductions in the GATT rounds have disrupted some Canadian industries but most dislocations in the past have been anticipated and assistance had been designed to help. In the case of free trade with the United States, the loss of manufacturing jobs has been visible enough but not the matching adjustment assistance. The adverse impact has been yet more visible as a result of being concentrated in specific areas of manufacturing and in specific communities that remain unaware of any effort to assist them to cope with the inevitable dislocation.
Some part of the all too evident job loss is a result of new international competition and a global recession and of continuing fiscal excess at home and an overly enthusiastic anti-inflationary policy in Ottawa, bringing with it high interest rates and a greatly inflated Canadian dollar. However, some part of the job loss is as a result of the absence of effective adjustment assistance, especially with regard to the access to capital by small businesses whose equity base is too weak to borrow against.
The need for innovative measures to assist small businesses to do their jobs was well identified by the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre when it said in its recent report: "The continuous innovation and investment required to support a high value-added

economy will not occur without supportive financial assistance".
Even in this area of trade policy the government's work is at best half finished. Only the most sanguine among us today would argue that the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement has lived up to the extravagant promises made by the government in 1988. Its central justification was to secure access to the American market in the face of rising U.S. protectionism, yet a whole series of recent trade disputes have demonstrated just how tenuous that access is.
One of the principal reasons that the Liberal Party supported Canada's participation in the North American free trade negotiations was to correct shortcomings in the original Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. We called for tougher environmental and labour standards. We called for an accession clause to make it easier for other countries to join and thus to expand Canada's free trade options beyond the United States. Most important, we called for the inclusion of a subsidies and anti-dumping code, one which would put to an end the kind of trade harassment that has been eroding the free trade environment between the two countries and that would introduce a badly needed degree of predictability in our entry into the yet untested waters of Mexico.
As the House knows, there remains a great flaw in the NAFTA, or a black hole at the centre, which threatens to undermine the success of the entire regime. That is the continuing absence of a common set of trading rules. Not only is there no definition of subsidies in the agreement or a commitment to replace countervail action with competition law, but even the agreement's modest provision to pursue these objectives with in a specified time has been quietly dropped in the NAFTA, to be replaced by a woolly commitment to pursue the goal in some future consultations.
It is most important and most regrettable that there is an absence of common trading rules embedded in either the FTA or the NAFTA. In the long run it will undermine the legitimacy of the entire arrangement. The NAFTA is essentially a political document. However, its authority ultimately rests not on the letter of the text, but on the support it enjoys among the electorates of the three countries.
Nothing has done more to undermine enthusiasm in Canada for freer trade agreements than the highly public spectacle of ongoing punitive and seemingly groundless U.S. trade actions launched during the four years since the beginning of the supposed era of free trade with the United States. Beyond all others, it is this central question that must be addressed.
It is for that reason the Leader of the Opposition has called for amendments to the North American free trade agreement. "A Liberal government", he has said, "will seek changes to the agreement and to the North American free trade agreement". He went on: "Unlike the Conservatives, we know an opportunity when we see one. There is a new administration in Washington. It has said it wants to reopen a number of these same areas. A Liberal government will take it up on that. Not only will we seize opportunities", the leader continued, "we will create new opportunities. If it is inevitable that a western hemisphere trade bloc evolves, Canada must play an active and independent role in defining that bloc instead of always reacting to Washington's hub-and-spoke approach to trade in this hemisphere".
"Canada", he concluded, "should be working with other countries to minimize dominance by the stronger partner. While we must seize the opportunity to have trade in the Americas, a Liberal government will not turn its back on the rest of the world. The fastest growing economies in the world are in the Pacific basin. The current government has ignored that region although Canada is a Pacific basin nation. A Liberal administration will put a high priority on existing trade with that dynamic region".
For the reasons that I have touched upon and others that would be easy to elaborate on, I want to move an amendment to the motion before the House.
I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all words after the word

Mr. Speaker, there are strange things going on with the Conservatives. The Prime Minister says his party is in great shape financially while headlines consistently confirm that the country is in an economic mess.

The Titanic ship of state is on a course at full speed headed irreversibly for the mother of all icebergs in the midst of the storm of the century with no radar. THE CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there can be no doubt that the free trade agreement has been very beneficial to Canada's agricultural sector.
In fact, exports of durum wheat to the United States have increased 52 per cent since 1988 while exports of refined canola oil are up 77 per cent.
The success of the FTA is augmented by the inclusion of the dispute settlement mechanism which has yielded one positive result after another.
Recently the FTA panel report on exports of durum wheat rejected American allegations that our wheat is shipped into the United States at unfairly low prices.
In fact the panel ruled that the practices of the Canadian Wheat Board and the Western Grain Transportation Act are within the bounds of the free trade agreement.
History will show that this government made the right choice in its adoption of a policy of freer trade.

Mr. Speaker, in 1987 the Government of Canada, in a policy statement entitled Sharing Our Future, said that its top priority is the alleviation of poverty in the Third World. Last June at the earth summit in Rio the government promised new and additional aid to help poor nations in Africa and elsewhere.

Mr. Speaker, in its report on the St. Lawrence seaway the transport committee recognized that the seaway system is dependent upon eastbound grain traffic for its survival.
There is evidence that the current method of payment of the western grain transportation subsidy is distorting the natural directional flow of grain shipments. As such, the committee recommended that until various discrepancies caused by the Western Grain Transportation Act are dealt with, the subsidy should be extended to include grain export movements through the seaway.
I believe that the subsidy is causing a directional bias in the shipment of grain in this country to the detriment of the seaway system. This distortion not only affects grain traffic flowing east but also has an effect on cargoes that move in a westerly direction through the seaway, such as iron ore. This further impacts on a steel industry that is already suffering.
Changes are being considered in the Western Grain Transportation Act. These changes must take into consideration transportation issues in addition to the welfare of our western farmers. I ask the government to eliminate the current directional bias that is having such a great impact on the St. Lawrence seaway.

Mr. Speaker, today is World Consumer Rights Day as proclaimed by the International Organization of Consumer Unions. This year's theme concerns transnational corporations and consumer interests. not include chicken cordon bleu, breaded chicken cordon blue, chicken Kiev, chicken breaded Kiev, boneless Rock Cornish with rice, stuffed Rock Cornish, boneless chicken, chicken Romanov, chicken Neptune, chicken TV dinners, old roosters and spent fowl. My question is for the minister of trade. speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:

The Bush administration turned down those proposals. The Clinton administration has said that it is willing to talk about the Canadian proposals. This is the basis on which we will be going into the negotiations later this week.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The Clinton administration has told the government that it wants an arrangement on import surges and that trade actions should be permitted where environmental standards are not enforced.
The government has acknowledged that were this to proceed it would mean that the NAFTA deal would have to be reopened.
My question is again directed to the minister of trade. Clearly this is not a deal that has been completed. Yet the government insists on putting it before the House of Commons when there are many other negotiations taking place that will fundamentally affect the deal itself.
Will the Minister for International Trade and his government not remove this piece of legislation from the House of Commons until Canadian people and members of the House of Commons really know what they are voting and debating?

Oral Questions

speechtext:

Furthermore, why does the government not recognize the need to present a total agreement to the House of Commons and to Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:

The legislative process in Canada has been under way with the hearings that have been held. It has been also under way in the United States. The negotiation on the terms of the implementing legislation in the United States is also under way. It will commence on April 1 in the Mexican Congress. The processes are all under way at about the same time.
I also want to underscore the point that the NAFTA, the agreement we signed on December 17, is a good deal in itself. It is for that reason we want to tie that one down and make sure we have the approval of the Parliament of Canada to ensure we get the full benefits of the agreement.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister for International Trade said that in any negotiations surrounding the North American free trade agreement: "A country has to be willing to give something in order to get something".
Now that the United States has reopened negotiations by demanding three parallel accords, could the minister explain what the Americans are willing to give in exchange for their three parallel accords, in exchange for Canadian government support? Is the Canadian government seeking a parallel accord on subsidies, a code which, for example, the C.D. Howe Institute in the last few days has again emphasized is critical to the success of any free trade agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Tbade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:

It is those proposals that we are pressing hard through the GATT negotiations. I would say to my hon. friend that by having these side agreements we are getting things that we sought in February 1992. They will not result in changes to the NAFTA that was signed on December 17.

The minister knows that the parallel accords will modify or in some ways alter the content and the terms of NAFTA. Otherwise, they would be meaningless. They would have no purpose. If the United States government attaches such importance to its three parallel accords it must be

asking the Canadian and the Mexican governments to support it on those three parallel accords. I ask the minister, what are Canada's interests? Why does the Canadian government not advance a proposal for a parallel accord in an area of prime concern to Canada, the subsidies code?

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we proposed changes in the subsidies code we would be reopening the agreement. What we put forward as of February 1992, and which will be reiterated at the meetings on Wednesday, are proposals that we believe are important in the relationships on the environment and on labour in particular.
Let me remind my hon. friend that there are five areas that Mr. Kantor has said are the object of U.S. interest: border clean-up between Mexico and the United States, nothing to do with Canada; stronger enforcement of national laws, primarily focused on Mexico; North American commissions on environment and labour standards which are the two areas that Canada proposed in February 1992 so that it is a continuation of the Canadian agenda; and worker adjustment and retraining, which is a matter between the U.S. administration and U.S. Congress. It should be done because Canadian laws or Canadian training programs are about two to three times more generous than the U.S. laws. The fifth area is that of import surges and we are not sure precisely what the Americans have in mind on that one. We will know better as we go through these discussions later on this week.

been stalled for months. They could be resumed if the government extended a new line of credit.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:

This is a very important country in terms of the stability of the world and it is a country that has been a superpower.
We will be looking at all aspects of aid. We want to be as creative as we can. Mr. Speaker, it seems to us on this side that if the government was really sincere about helping Russia it would tackle the wheat issue. Resumption of wheat shipments would help cash-starved prairie farmers. It would provide employment to seaway workers and it would restore hope to the port of Churchill which is slowly dying under current government policies. Moreover the Russians, who are good customers, want more wheat shipped through the port of Churchill. So what is it, an offer to help the Russians or just talk?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is definitely not just talk. On a per capita basis Canada has been among the most generous of western countries and we will continue to be in the forefront of what needs to be done.
I think it is also important to know that those have been commercial arrangements with Russia in the past that have gone on for some 35 years and they will continue to exist in the future.

March 15, 1993
Oral Questions
There is obviously some bridging needed but it is also important to indicate to the Russians and to the Russian people that the economic reforms and the economic disciplines are important as well. We are going to be there for Russia and we are going to be there to ensure that economic reform and democratic reform proceed in Russia.

When we get a full report then we will be actively considering the most imaginative and creative programs that we can bring forward to help Russia and the other countries of the former Soviet Union as well.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:

The Minister of Finance brought forward what I believe and what most people believe to be a very responsible statement in December, giving modest help to the economy while at the same time keeping in mind the fiscal constraints in which we are operating.
One of the things the New Democratic Party's economic plan does not factor in is all these things they are going to walk away from like the free trade agreement, the NAFTA and the GST. They are not factored into their over-all plans. Once those are factored in to the over-all plans, again it is typical Alice in Wonderland financial policies of the no down payment party.

March 15, 1993

In fact, it is the beginning of privatization. Canadians want to know, students in particular, what will be the future eligibility requirements for student loans? Who will establish the requirements and what will be the role of the banks in the establishment of those requirements?
