Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
For the fourth year in a row the government of Azerbaijan has continued its blockade of Armenia. This winter has found the people of Armenia suffering extreme hardships. Many have died. With the melting snow and floods of spring, epidemics can be anticipated to rage out of control. This desperate situation has reached a crisis.
Will the Canadian government move quickly to ask for an urgent meeting of the United Nations Security Council to address this critical situation to find a way to force the removal of the blockade of Armenia thereby allowing food, medical supplies and fuel to reach these desperate people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say first that like others the Canadian government is very concerned about the situation in Armenia and what has happened there over the past few years. We have taken a strong role in the CSCE in trying to bring about a solution in a series of negotiations that might help to bring this situation to an end.
I appreciate the hon. member's suggestion that this should come before the Security Council. I do want to report to him that through the CSCE, in part because Canada began the process in the CSCE well over a year ago, there was a bit of a breakthrough last Thursday in
terms of bringing people to the table. There was a meeting in Vienna. There will be an eight-member mission to Armenia and Azerbaijan to lay the groundwork for negotiations in the future working toward a ceasefire.
That has not stopped us from urging that all the parties bring this to a solution, nor has it stopped us from giving humanitarian aid to Armenia and to others in the region to try to alleviate the immediate suffering.
We will not hesitate to propose taking it to the Security Council should the CSCE efforts fail. However, we think we are seeing a breakthrough at the moment.

Europe, the government has a fiscal situation which applies to everything including the budgets with respect to sports. I am sure that with my hon. colleague's support, we will get a response from the government to the task force which makes recommendations to deal with such issues.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36(8), I have the honour to table, in both official languages, the government's response to four petitions.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition to present from Canadians who are asking that the Parliament of Canada regulate the use of foul language and violence on radio and television.
They point out that foul language need not be used to entertain in English or in French.

They also emphasized that violence, either in the form of acts of violence or inappropriate language, undermines the efforts of parents and society.

I have another petition here from Regina and Winnipeg about the GST on books and learning materials.

These petitioners deplore the fact that there is a goods and services tax on books and reading materials. They point out there has never been such a tax before. They feel it goes against one of our fundamental principles as
a democratic state and that reading and literacy are cornerstones of societies such as our own.
They also accentuate the need to make sure we have a literate and numerate society in order to be competitive and increasingly productive. They ask the government to remove this tax.

Mr. Speaker, I have two petitions from residents of my riding of York West who are petitioning this Parliament, and particularly the government, to rescind Bill C-91, the pharmaceutical legislation that did away with the compulsory drug licensing system.
Over the weekend we in Toronto had a very impressive public debate on the future health care system of this country. One main point that repeatedly came up was the increasing price of prescription drugs. Just when the Americans are beginning to see the light and contemplate copying the old system, we in this country are doing away with compulsory drug licensing, allowing prices to increase, increasing the cost of health care, and discouraging Canadian entrepreneurs and Canadian pharmaceutical companies from doing well in Canada and across the globe.
Therefore the petitioners are hopeful the government, perhaps under a new leadership that we will soon see, will take a second look at pharmaceutical legislation that has clearly hurt the Canadian interest.

Mr. Speaker,
I have close to 800 names on two petitions from my riding. The petitions are submitted in the memory of a little girl, Dawn Shaw, who was raped and murdered in the Comox valley.
The petitioners note that the present justice system fails to protect the children of our communities who are increasingly becoming victims of sexual assault. They make a number of suggestions for parliamentarians.
They suggest that judges should not be allowed to drop sexual assault charges because of delays in bringing a case to trial and that the jail sentence for sexual assault offenders should be lengthened for any person convicted. They also suggest that the police be permitted to take DNA samples from persons suspected of sexual assault and that DNA imprints of paedophiles and sex offenders be kept on a national police database.
March 15, 1993

They propose that sex offenders should undergo monitoring by police when they are released from jail, even after parole, that paedophiles and sex offenders should be required to register with police in their communities of residence, and that the police should be required to contact schools and other agencies dealing with children regarding the whereabouts of such paedophiles and sex offenders.
The undersigned residents of Canada, in memory of Dawn Shaw, request that Parliament enact legislation to change the justice system to provide greater protection for children from sexual assault and to assure conviction of offenders.

Mr. Speaker, I have petitions that were prepared by the British Heritage Institute of Canada and are signed by almost 1,200 people.
They acknowledge the fact that Canada has adopted a policy of official multiculturalism, allowing peoples of all racial origins and ethnic backgrounds the opportunity to retain and enjoy their native heritages. They acknowledge as well the fact that funding has been provided to allow multiple heritage actions and activities and yet there have been no such provisions for those of British origin or background to secure their heritage.
They indicate there is a strong conception among many Canadians that multicultural provisions do not apply to Canadians of British heritage. They call upon Parliament to take whatever action is necessary to ensure that the provisions of official multiculturalism apply equally to all ethnic groups regardless of origin.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I have the privilege of presenting to Parliament petitions signed by many of my constituents.
The undersigned petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to accept legislation designed to eliminate violence against women and children, to support women and children who report incidents of assault or abuse, to provide assistance and support for women and children reporting assault or abuse, to provide relief and support to women as mothers to protect their children,

to concentrate special effort on the training of lawyers, medical and therapeutic communities, court workers, judges and police to become knowledgeable about women and child abuse, and to emphasize the need for realistic and adequate child support orders and enforcement to focus public attention on this very important and long ignored problem.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition signed by many people in my riding.

This petition is with regard to a board game. Parents and grandparents seek a ban on the new game to be introduced in Canada called serial killer board game, first edition. The game comes with a body bag, 25 babies and four serial killer figures. Its object is to commit murder and the person with the highest body count is the winner.
The game is not in the best interests of children and in the wrong hands could become dangerous and suggestive to easily impressed young people.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament and I support them whole-heartedly, to urge the Government of Canada to ban the sale of the serial killer game and prevent any other such game or material to be made available in Canada in order to protect innocent children.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his insightful and comprehensive address with respect to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and NAFTA and for his questions in the House today.
I want to ask three very quick questions. The first one is with respect to the amendment. Does infrastructure refer in any part to education, training and retraining programs?
March 15, 1993

The second one relates to his mention of the black hole. As I understood it he was referring to common trade rules, the lack of definition of subsidies and anti-dumping rules, and the insistence I believe by our party-and I would like some confirmation of this-of protection of our energy sources, our labour standards, and our environmental standards. Would my colleague from Etobicoke North in fact address these particular issues?
A final point is that he did make very clear the difference between our party and the governing party. Perhaps he could say a word on what the differences are between our party and the party to my left. I would appreciate that.

Mr. Speaker, on the question of whether infrastructure includes training and retraining, yes, indeed. Central to our policy going into government will be to emphasize the ways in which Canadians can be helped to benefit from freer trade, whether it be global or hemispheric. That includes the necessity for much more effective training and retraining programs as supported by labour and government as outlined, for example, in the recent report of the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre.
Second, dealing with subsidies, the black hole that I spoke of and which the member has in mind is the absence of any agreement on trade remedy law or, to put it another way, on what is a subsidy. There is a need to fill that hole to complete what is unfinished business. The opportunity is there, presented by the American interest today in parallel accords. Why not seek a parallel accord with the United States and Mexico based on the proposed GATT wording with regard to subsidies and take that as a Canadian initiative to improve our opportunities in the world of freer trade?
Third, on energy, our party is committed to protecting Canada's energy interests in accordance with our international obligations. It will remain a principal concern as we review all questions surrounding freer trade on a hemispheric or on a global basis.
Finally, I thank the hon. member for his kind words and appreciate his continuing involvement in the further definition of the areas of prime interest to Canadians in the question of freer trade.

I have a short question, Mr. Speaker.
Yesterday during Question Period the leader of the Liberal Party when asked about how the GST would be replaced twice mentioned the manufacturers' sales tax which existed before the GST. I wanted to ask the member who has just spoken for the Liberals if this indicated that the Liberal Party is now looking at the manufacturers' sales tax as one of the replacements for the GST?

Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House regard the goods and services tax as flawed and as having been introduced at the most inauspicious time imaginable, exactly when the Conservative government did so.
With regard to alternatives, it is the commitment of our leader and our party to review the issue in a parliamentary committee when we form the government and give to that committee a mandate to review all aspects of taxation questions and to report back to the House within a year.

Mr. Speaker, let me start, if I could, by giving the House and the people of the country some sense of just how seriously we see the decline this economy has experienced in the past period of years.
Frankly, we see a devastating reduction in economic opportunity and, most important, the elimination of hundreds of thousands of jobs in manufacturing, but not just in manufacturing. There has been a record number of bankruptcies across the services sector. There are serious problems in the farm sector of this economy, and the resources sector has run into considerable difficulty.
It is quite clear that under this government's leadership we do not see prosperity developing or movement toward full employment, which are so crucial for Canadians across this land.
We have tried to put forward a counter-position to the government's approach. Each time we say to the government that it must do something different it says: This is it, this is the only direction we can take; we have to stay the course, we have to keep to this path because it is the right approach. It has kept saying that as unemployment has mounted, as the numbers on the welfare rolls have

March 15, 1993
Supply
mounted, and as the misery of many Canadians has become worse and worse.
We do not believe that just staying the course is a proper response to one of the worst recessions that we have seen in this country. We do not believe that it is a proper response to one of the weakest recoveries we have seen in this country, a recovery which has been called a jobless recovery. It is such a contradiction in terms that there should be a jobless recovery. For us the only recovery which makes sense is a recovery that puts people back to work and lets families again feel a sense of hope about their future.
What is the different approach that we would take? It is based on three crucial points. First, we believe that it is time to stop following the Reagan-Thatcher-Mulroney approach of trickle-down economics, which says we should give huge new tax breaks to those at the top of our income structure and load new taxes, like the goods and services tax, on those in the middle and then somehow expect that new growth and new prosperity will result for everyone.
This trickle-down approach has not worked in the United States, where it has vastly increased the differential between rich and poor in that country. It has not worked in Britain, where the British economy has found itself limping badly in comparison to its European partners. It has certainly not worked here in this country, where a trickle-down approach has simply meant an increase in poverty, an increase in joblessness, and an increase in the welfare rolls across this country.
We think it is important to instead have a trickle-up approach which gives the tax benefits to that 80 per cent of the population that has been hit so hard by this government and so badly deserves some tax breaks for the future.
We want to have those at the top of the income system pay not an exorbitant share but their fair share of what is required as revenues in this society.
Let us stop giving the benefits to those at the top and give benefits to the vast majority in our economy through the tax system and then let those benefits trickle up and give us prosperity that way.
Second, it is time to stop tying ourselves so closely to the United States and hoping that foreign investment from the United States will solve our economic problems in Canada, hoping that we can attract new capital and new entrepreneurs to come in from the United States and give us a set of new jobs for our people and new opportunities. If we have learned anything from the free trade deal, from this experience of relying on the United States, it is that we cannot depend on what happens to the south of us to give us a future in Canada.
We need to tiy out our own freedom as an advanced, high-technology economy able to use measures such as Canadian content laws, which we are stopped from using under the free trade deal, to build new jobs in this country and establish trade ties with the entire world, not just to increase our ties with the United States.
Finally, third, it is time to stop attacking the unemployed as the Conservatives have done with their changes to the unemployment insurance system and as the Liberals did in the last recession when they attacked the unemployed in exactly the same way. It is time to say that the problem in a recession does not lie with the unemployed. The problem is unemployment, the joblessness that has been created as part of these recessionary conditions.
We need a jobs first strategy. That is why we have brought before the country and we bring before this House this strategy for a full employment economy, a jobs plan for Canada from the national New Democratic Party. It is a plan that would show us how to stop this trickle-down approach and how to free ourselves from the United States trade deal and improve our world trade ties. It shows us how we can create half a million additional jobs over the next five years for a total of between one and a half and two million jobs to be created in this country. That is an extra half million over what the different projections suggest we might achieve with the present approach.
This is not a plan that would achieve Utopia in a first parliamentary term. It is a plan that would give us a significant reduction in our unemployment rate to about 7 per cent. That is not good enough but it is much better than the 9 per cent to 10 per cent unemployment rate projected by all the economic forecasters if we continue to follow the present plan this government is following.
March 15, 1993

At the heart of this plan is a commitment to the step-by-step elimination of the goods and services tax. In our first budget we would remove the GST from four or five key areas that have important job benefits for the country. In our second budget we would reduce the GST from 7 per cent to 5 per cent. In our third and fourth budgets we would reduce it to first 4 per cent and then to 3 per cent. In our final budget, under this plan, we would eliminate that final 3 per cent of GST.
We would do so because we think it is a bad tax. It is a tax that hurts small business. It is a tax that kills jobs. It is a tax that damages the drive to improve our economy. It is a tax that hurts consumption. It is a tax that hurts our border communities.
Taking this step-by-step approach would permit a big job push at the start of our plan, partly through job gains from eliminating the GST step by step and partly through initiatives that would come from cutting existing expenditures, especially in the area of defence.
It is also important to recognize that moving forward with the elimination of the goods and services tax would stop our cost of living from rising as quickly as it otherwise would.
This would mean a lower rate of interest and that means lower expenditures on the interest payments that we have to make on our national debt.
About 25 per cent of our replacement for the goods and services tax would come from extra employment. Another 25 per cent would come from cutting expenditures. The final 50 per cent, to get rid of the GST, would come from making our tax system fair through three steps.
First, we must see to it that four existing and damaging loopholes in our tax system that help the large-scale corporations and benefit the wealthy in this country are plugged. We would change the present system that allows corporations to deduct interest payments so that they can then take the loans that they are taking out and invest them in foreign countries. We would plug the possibility that exists for corporations to deduct their entertainment under the present tax system. We would change the capital gains tax system so that the unfair

benefits for the wealthy no longer exist. We would see to it that there are steps taken so that the family trusts set up over many years under the Liberals and under the Conservatives start to have to pay the capital gains taxes they owe. That is one set of changes to make the tax system fairer.
A second set of changes would be to put into effect a wealth transfer tax. This is something they have in the United States. This requires that when people receive inheritances from estates of over, let us say, $500,000, or $1 million as it is in the United States, they pay normal tax on the income which they get from those inheritances. Again, this is something that is perfectly straightforward and fair and something the U.S. has had in effect.
Finally, we see it as crucial the benefits that have been established by both Liberals and Conservatives in the income tax system should change. These are benefits that give tremendous handouts to those at the very top of our income structure. People whose individual income is over $100,000 per year would pay income tax on that last amount over $100,000 at a rate of 35 per cent federally instead of the present rate of 29 per cent. Those whose individual income is over $135,000 would pay at the rate of 40 per cent instead of the present 29 per cent.
These changes would make it possible to completely replace the GST, to establish an extra 500,000 jobs and to reduce the level of deficit over the next parliamentary term by $11 billion.
It is not just New Democrats who claim this. We have had this plan tested and tested carefully by an independent organization that even Conservative spokespeople have said do a good job in making these kinds of assessments. Informetrica has said that this will work and will achieve the goals that I have been talking about. By achieving these goals we will put this economy back on the road to recovery.
We will do it as my leader has suggested today by recognizing that there is a human deficit and not just a fiscal deficit in this country. To attack that fiscal deficit we must attack the human deficit too. We must do so by getting people back to work. We must do so by making

our tax system fair. We must do so by being honest and up front about exactly what we would do in government.
This disappoints me the most about my friends in the Liberal Party in opposition. I would have hoped that they would have been challenged by the issuing of our plan last month to issue something that says what they will do about the GST, free trade and the NAFTA.
Elowever, this is not so. On the GST we just heard the spokesperson for the Liberal Party say that the Liberals will set up a committee after they are elected to sort things out and come back with an answer after a year. There you have it, ladies and gentlemen across the country. Vote for the Liberal Party and you might know what you get after a year.
The same spokesperson has said that they want to renegotiate the NAFTA and the free trade agreement but they do not say what they will do if they do not succeed in everything they want in their renegotiation. They do not say: "We need this or else we would scrap it. We do not need that in order to stay in". They simply say: "Trust us just as in the past". They want you to trust them as in 1974 when the Liberal Party ran a magnificent election campaign and said to the people of this country that it was a terrible idea to freeze wages: "It is a terrible idea to have a wage freeze. It is terribly unfair so we will not do it. We are against it". Then, when they were elected, they put that very wage freeze into effect a short eight months later.
I say to the people of this country that they should not trust the Liberals again. Do not give us nine more years of Conservative rule. Adopt the jobs plan of the New Democrats and we can put people back to work and make this country work once more.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention to my hon. friend, the member for Essex-Windsor. While I do not always agree with everything he says I must give him credit, as my leader and our Prime Minister has said, because at least his party has clear and unequivocal policies.
I know there are individual members of the Liberal Party, like the member for Broadview-Greenwood, who have put forward many policies, as has the member for Etobicoke North. In fact, I have never understood why
the member for Etobicoke North sits on that side of the House since he supports the policies of this government.
In any event I want to address two questions to my hon. friend because I find myself somewhat confused with some of the things that he and his colleagues have been saying. In particular I want to ask him about this oft-repeated proposal that they have to not allow businesses to deduct as tax expense items hospitality and lunches and so on. This is notwithstanding the fact that I have noticed that when various organizations around the country have come to Ottawa and put on receptions the New Democratic Party members are glad to avail themselves of those receptions.
Here is my specific question with respect to that. Can my hon. friend tell me what studies his party has done that will show the impact of such a proposal on the hospitality industry in Canada and could he table these in this House? How many restaurants in our cities will go out of business, for example? How many hotels will go out of business? Clearly a major part of the business done by restaurants and hotels in the hospitality industry in this country is business related. I know my hon. friend would not suggest that such a proposal, if implemented, would not have an absolutely devastating effect on the hospitality industry in this country.
I would ask him to advise us about the studies they have done. I would ask and invite him to table those studies in this House.

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the various receptions that take place here, I think that those reception are paid for out of money they have raised. Various organizations such as the Federation of Canadian Municipalities that raise money and put on receptions do not get a subsidy from the taxpayer. There is no subsidy that the Federation of Canadian Municipalities gets from the taxpayer. There is no subsidy that the trade unions get for any reception they put on. There is no subsidy for the Canadian Federation of Agriculture if it puts on a reception.
However, when the Canadian Petroleum Association comes here and puts on a reception it is able to deduct money that is spent by individual firms that help sponsor it from what is paid in taxes. One always notices on the
March 15, 1993

program that there are certain individual firms that helps sponsor the reception.
I do not think people realize what this means. It means that instead of paying a full level of corporation tax on their profits the money is taken and spent on this reception. It comes right off the amount that would have been paid as taxes to the people of Canada. This means that each and every one of us as taxpayers across this country is subsidizing Imperial Oil, Shell Canada, or the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Royal Bank, or some of the biggest, richest companies in this country, to wine and dine members of Parliament. With all due respect, I think these companies are sufficiently rich that they ought to be able to pay the amounts involved.
The member has suggested that surely there will be damage done to the tourist and hospitality industry. I want to tell the member who raised this question that it has become virtually impossible for me to go out and visit a restaurant in my constituency in the Windsor area because restaurant after restaurant has just been hammered by the goods and services tax. If you ask any of those restaurants if they would prefer to have the hospitality deduction kept or if they would prefer to have the GST eliminated, there is no question that their answer would be to get rid of the goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, the 300 restaurants in my riding will appreciate hearing that the NDP is doubting the legitimacy of a true business expense in their restaurants. To me it is just beyond comprehension. Elowever, I do not want to focus on that. I have a lot of respect for the finance critic of the New Democratic Party.
In the centre of my riding on a side street is Hampton Variety. This variety store is operated by a young entrepreneur whose name is Terry McAdorey. The basis for his work is the community, not competition. He bakes his own muffins and bread. He makes his own soups and stews. He buys his cheeses from small family farms. He is the spirit of neighbourly love in the community. He employs and encourages young people. He represents a contrast to the existence one experiences when working for a transnational corporation.

It seems to me that we need to revisit and review the contribution of community-based work as a contrast to the type of work that is imposed upon us because of these exercises in the free trade agreement and NAFTA. Could the New Democratic member give his party's position on that community-based work and its importance to the economy?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question. I am not sure whether I have told my friend this before but I started in politics by canvassing in Broadview in the first election of the New Democrats back in 1965.1 know his constituency well.
He mentioned the many small restaurants and I ate in a lot of them when I was part of that community. I know those restaurants would be much more concerned with the elimination of the goods and services tax and the benefits that would bring to them than with the potential benefits business deductions bring.
After all, we already treat deductions for business luncheons differently. We only permit the deduction of 80 per cent of them. That shows there is something we are a little suspicious of with respect to them to begin with.
The second point he raised is an excellent one. Part of our effort with this plan and with a number of the approaches to changing the economy we have tried to put forward over the last four or five years have been to say that we have to start looking at economic development from the bottom up instead of the top down.
Now that includes establishing things like a national investment fund which my leader talked about this morning. This would be of particular benefit to small business. It gives small business people the potential for access to capital which they so rarely have at the moment without having to mortgage houses or, it almost seems sometimes, having to mortgage their families.
That is important but we also see as part of our jobs plan a crucial emphasis on community development. We see the establishment of community development organizations and support for community development groups. We see support for co-operatives and credit unions based in the community as all part of that same effort to build from the ground up. This is instead of assuming everything will flow from some great new enterprise that is attracted in from the outside. Yes, that

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate. I am glad the New Democratic Party has put the broad spectre of economic issues before the House and the nation today because I think these are things that are very much on the minds of Canadians. These are issues that should be debated seriously and frequently in this House.
The particular motion the New Democratic Party has put forward causes me some concern. It seems to me it is in conflict with itself. When one talks about an economic recovery program that must endorse a strategy for full employment which entails abrogating the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and not implementing the North American free trade agreement, it seems to me that those concepts are very directly in conflict with themselves. They do not seem to make any sense at all. I do not know how the New Democratic Party proposes that our economy and the standard of living of Canadians should grow if we are going to turn our backs on the opportunities to sell the products that are the absolute basis of that growth.
I listened earlier today when the leader of the New Democratic Party spoke. She talked about not being dependent on the North American market. She talked about reaching out to other markets in other parts of the world.
With the greatest respect, that is precisely what Canadian business people are doing. They are doing it already and they do not need the government to suggest to them that they should do that. They know perfectly well where their market opportunities are. They want the government to create the climate and the opportunity in which trade growth can take place. Through trade we have an opportunity to see economic development in this country. This country is a trading nation, first and foremost.
A couple of realities have been ignored by my hon. friends in the New Democratic Party in the position they have taken with respect to the free trade agreement and the NAFTA. I would love to have an opportunity to discuss a number of the issues that are included within
the resolutions they have put forward. Time will not permit it so I am going to focus on these trade issues.
First, I think the New Democratic Party has to realize that the Canadian market is not big enough to sustain the standard of living that Canadians expect. It is as simple as that. We export a quarter of what we produce in this country. We must have access to markets abroad.
We have only one alternative if we are going to build big walls around Canada and turn down the opportunity to trade abroad. Realistically, we are not going to trade abroad unless we wake up to the reality of global competitiveness. Then we have only to sell internally in Canada.
If we are ever going to achieve full employment, which the New Democratic Party says is its goal and aspiration, then the only way we are going to do that is to have the government put everybody on the payroll.
That would not work either. The Liberal Party tried that for 15 years and we know what the outcome was. You just spend yourself into a cycle of debt and nine years later we are still trying to dig ourselves out. I have a feeling there will not be too many of us left in this House by the time we do get around to digging ourselves out of that cycle of debt which was imposed on us by 15 years of irresponsible spending by the previous government.
The second reality the New Democratic Party is ignoring is what is happening in the world today. There is a change in trading patterns going on around the world. It is not just in this country or just on this continent, but indeed all over the world. Global trading blocs are developing. The nations of the world are negotiating new sets of trading rules. This will facilitate as well as liberalize trade around the world.
The name of the game, whether the New Democrats and the Canadian Labour of Congress-and I realize they are relatively indistinguishable-recognize it or not, is that the world is going to go on with or without us. What is in the interests of Canadians is that we be there and we be there to benefit in what is happening.
The New Democrats do not have to take it from me, this business about competitiveness. They think barriers can be erected around this country and high wage levels can be protected forever but it will not work. You have to be able to sell your products. You cannot sell your products, quite simply, unless you can offer competitive prices. That is the name of the game from now on
March 15, 1993

whether we like it or not. Anyone who doubts that does not have to take it from me.
Just look at the phenomenon of cross-border shopping that has gone on. We tell people to buy Canadian. What have Canadians done? They say: "I will buy where I get the best deal". If that is in Buffalo, Seattle or Bangor, that is where they are going to shop.
The only way we are going to be competitive within our own market is the same basis on which we are going to be competitive abroad. That is the fundamental weakness. Building walls simply will not work because our market is not big enough to sustain the economy we wish to live by.
When the New Democratic Party leader suggests, as she did earlier today, that we should look to other markets I cannot help but reflect on what I hear her trade critic saying time and time again when he talks about low-wage Mexicans taking away the jobs of Canadians. This is the great fear of the NAFTA we are told. In 1988 we were told by both opposition parties that the entire Canadian economy would grind to a halt because of the free trade agreement. That was because people in Alabama were ready to work for lower wages than people in Canada. That has not been the case. We have been through a recession. It has been tough. It has been tough not just in Canada but all around the world.
The truth of the matter is if low-wage Mexicans were going to be putting us all out of work why is the leader of the New Democratic Party talking about seeking out new markets in Asia, Africa and all these other places? Does she think with respect to the Philippines, Thailand, India or Senegal that there is any difference between low wage rates in those countries and Mexico? Of course not. We are able to compete with the best of them.
Look at our trade with Japan, one of our biggest trading partners. Wage rates are higher in Japan than they are here. Europe is a major trading partner. Wage rates in Europe are as high or higher than they are here.
What constitutes ability to compete in the marketplace is not simply wage rates but competitiveness. That is what it is all about. That is a concept that the New
Supply
Democratic Party does not seem to fully and adequately understand.
We do have to seek access to new markets. Europe is creating its bloc of 12 countries and that is possibly going to grow. Eastern Europe has IFTA. There are the trade developments in southeast Asia. What better opportunity is there for Canadians than to be part of the largest trading market in the world, which is that created by the North American free trade agreement? It is an opportunity and it has worked. The concept has worked in the past.
I would simply cite the example of the auto pact which was created in 1965. I might say it was roundly and thoroughly opposed by the New Democratic Party of the day and by the Canadian Labour Congress and the United Auto Workers, as they were then, now the CAW. All were opponents of the auto pact when it was brought in. They do not feel that way now. It is a sacrosanct thing as far as Canadian auto workers are concerned.
I suppose if we come back here 20 to 25 years from now we will hear the NDP standing up and taking the credit for the North American free trade agreement. Its members will be saying it was all their idea in the first place. That is what we are going to see.
This business of losing jobs to Mexicans is something we hear time and time again. It is time that my friends in the New Democratic Party realized that what really counts is the unit cost of production. That is what is significant. Labour is a component of that. It is true that on average, labour costs are 7.5 times lower in Mexico than they are in Canada. However, what is the other side of the equation? The other side of the equation is productivity. Productivity is 6.5 times higher in Canada than it is in Mexico.
In addition to that, the cost of capital is lower in Canada. A business cannot be run without money. Money is more accessible here. Capital productivity is higher. We get more out of our technology and our equipment here than they do in Mexico. Add it all up. The result very simply is that Canadian workers and Canadian companies can compete with the best the Mexicans have to offer.

Therefore, NAFTA gives us the opportunity to access a market of 85 million people that is largely closed to us today.
If the Mexicans were going to put us all out of business then we would be out of business now. Most of the goods that come to Canada from Mexico come in tariff free now, so why have the Mexicans not supplanted us already? On the other hand, virtually everything that we wish to sell in Mexico is either completely blocked through import licensing restrictions or must come through a 20 per cent tariff.
The facts, and I know sometimes my hon. friends opposite do not like to have facts injected into discussions, sustain the argument that the North American free trade agreement in this context is very good.
I want to talk for a minute about trade in general. I want to talk a little bit about my own part of Canada, Nova Scotia and more particularly the south shore. Trade has been the lifeblood of Canada but also of the maritimes. If we go back in the history of this country and of my region there was a time before Confederation when little old Nova Scotia, my province, had the fourth largest volume of shipping of any nation in the world. I know you knew that, Mr. Speaker, but I do not know if my hon. friends opposite knew that. Confederation came along and with it came tariff walls that disrupted the natural flow of trade between the Atlantic provinces, the maritime provinces, and the United States. Our economy has never really recovered from that blow.
Now we see the opportunity, and the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement has given us the opportunity, to re-establish those lines and the flow of trade that comes from them.
Look for example at my own constituency of South Shore where because of the kind of scaremongering by a lot of people there are many people in my area concerned about what the impact of free trade has really been and what the impact of the NAFTA will be.
Over 8,000 people in my constituency make their living from the fishery. My constituency has the highest volume of fish landings by value of any constituency in the country and that includes the ones in Newfoundland, and I see the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans here. I want to tell him that my constituency has the biggest
volume in value of landings of any constituency in the country and one-third of those landings goes to the United States. Access to that American market is critically important.
We have a paper mill. The Bowater Mersey paper mill employs over 800 people in South Shore and 60 per cent of the product of that plant goes to the United States. Sixty per cent of those 800 jobs are dependent on trade to the United States.
We have a Michelin Tires plant. I am told it is the most productive Michelin Tires plant in the world, in the entire Michelin system. We are very proud of that plant and we are even more proud of the workers in that plant, who are the best in the world according to Michelin. There are 1,400 jobs there and last week they celebrated the production of their 50 millionth tire. That is a tremendous thing. It has been wonderful for Nova Scotia. Two-thirds of that production goes to the United States.
You have heard me in this Flouse before, Mr. Speaker, talk about Christmas trees. We export 1.5 million Christmas trees a year from South Shore. There are some 500 people in South Shore who make their living from Christmas tree production, and 90 per cent of our Christmas trees go to the United States.
Then there is the tourist industry. There are a couple of thousand people employed in the hospitality industry and in the tourist industry. The American tourists that come up, particularly in the summer and fall, and the cruise ships that come up from the United States, create work for Nova Scotians. If we add it all up the conclusion that we come to is that trading links and the access to the United States and now to Mexico, which is the most important part of these agreements, are critically important to the economic development of our industry.
We do not have an historic trading relationship with the Mexicans but now that the NAFTA has come about and now that it has been signed we are finding increasing interest. All of a sudden we are discovering that there are new market opportunities for our processed fish. We are finding that there might even be opportunities for Canadian fishermen and fish companies to go down and assist the Mexicans in the harvesting of their own fish resources because to date the Mexicans have not had the technology and vessels to harvest their own fish resources. One of the solutions to our own fishing prob-
March 15, 1993

lems is to find fishing opportunities for our fleet and for our companies in assisting the Mexicans in developing their own area. Obviously we have a great new opportunity in terms of Christmas trees. The Mexicans celebrate Christmas and they have not been bringing in Christmas trees from Atlantic Canada.
I want to give the Mexicans due notice here today that we are going to be down there selling them some of the finest Christmas trees in the world because the finest Christmas trees in the world come from the south shore of Nova Scotia, as everybody in this House has come to know in recent times.
Then there are investment opportunities that flow from the access that we get under the FTA and indeed will get under the NAFTA. Companies that say they are interested in settling their plant and living in Canada, in particular in this case in Atlantic Canada where there is an excellent work force and the opportunity for a wonderful quality of life, are still going to have the opportunity to sell to that market of more than 350 million people in the United States and Mexico. The investment opportunities that are created by the NAFTA, on top of the success of the FTA are really quite encouraging.
My friends opposite sometimes entertain themselves by debunking the free trade agreement. We all know that we are not really going to know for another 10 to 15 years exactly how profoundly the free trade agreement has impacted this country, though it is very obvious that the initial signs show that it has been very positive. We have been through a difficult recession in this country and yet we have seen the benefits of the free trade agreement already starting to show in a serious way.
I would refer my hon. friends, who may not take as gospel everything I say though I cannot understand why, to the independent study done by the C.D. Howe Institute and released not so long ago. It shows that since the FTA Canada's trade balance with the United States has improved more than its trade balance with other regions.

The FTA has led to more trade between Canada and the United States. It also shows that in those sectors liberalized by the FTA exports have increased most, in particular those in non-resource-based manufacturing.
Merchandise exports to the United States have increased to record levels since the FTA, from $102.6 billion in 1988 to $122.3 billion in 1992. That is a 19.2 per cent increase. Exports in 1992 increased 13.6 per cent over 1991.
In other words, as a result of the free trade agreement we are seeing more business being done. Our exports to the United States are growing steadily under the FTA, notwithstanding the fact that we have been through a recession which would, generally speaking, have a negative impact on the economy. The same can be said with respect to our merchandise trade surplus with the U.S., which has grown by 27.3 per cent since a year ago.
I have so many more things I would like to say on this subject and I know my hon. friends would like to hear them but I will just make one last point about the FTA and its impact and the anticipated impact of the NAFTA and that is encouraging foreign direct investment. That means other people investing money in Canada. Investing money in Canada means creating jobs for Canadians. That is a good thing.
We have seen a significant growth in investment. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association survey of some 325 companies conducted early in 1992 found that nearly half the companies said they increased capital investments in Canada after the FTA was implemented. Only 9 per cent reduced their investment. Investment means jobs.
I could quote from various authorities on the success this agreement has had and the wonderful things that it has done for us, but let me say simply that what NAFTA does is provide us an opportunity to go beyond the FTA. There were some problems with the FTA and they have been sorted out in these negotiations. Canada got the things it was concerned about.
The key points about the NAFTA are: the auto pact remains the same; agriculture is the same except barriers will be removed against Canadian opportunities for export of grains, oilseeds, pork, fish, potatoes and processed foods; our supply management system is not

Mr. Speaker, the government member who just spoke talked about "creating jobs for Canadians" and also said that: "The free trade agreement did create some problems".

Plants have closed in this country, not all as a result of the free trade agreement but clearly on balance there has been disruption and dislocation and there have been fewer jobs created.
Then he has the gumption to say now that we are entering the NAFTA, based on their track record with the free trade agreement, we should basically trust them.
Obviously if we take 10 Canadians the vast majority of those 10 Canadians will not trust this government, not only for these reasons but for others, and will certainly not trust this government on the NAFTA given its track record on the free trade agreement.
Can the hon. member explain the rationale for why this party wishes to rush enabling legislation on the NAFTA through this Chamber at the same time that our American counterparts, President Clinton and his trade representative Mickey Kantor, have made it abundantly clear in the last number of days that they have no intention of proceeding with the NAFTA until the other side agreements are concluded?
My question is very simple: If the Americans can look after number one, namely defending their own workers, their own industry, and their questions about the environment, why are we, from a negotiating standpoint, heading right into this situation rather than standing back for a second and looking at the deal to determine where we can make it better and tighten up those areas on behalf of Canadian workers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course I would be delighted to answer my hon. friend's question but I wish to clarify some confusion that obviously exists in his mind with respect to the job situation.
It is obviously going to take time to totally sort it out. I know that in the last couple of years, as I think somebody in the opposition said, every sparrow that has fallen has been blamed on the free trade agreement. The fact of the matter is, now that we have figures in for 1992, my hon. friend should be aware that we have had a net increase of 118,000 jobs in Canada for 1991-92.
If he examines what is going on he will see that our recovery is being driven by exports, primarily by exports to the United States. If that is not the testimony my hon. friend needs I do not know what I can present him with.
Second, he raises questions about the environment, the parallel accords, and the process of ratification. By the way, Canadians know where this government stands on the NAFTA and they know where the New Democratic Party stands on the NAFTA but they are not too sure where the Liberal Party stands on the NAFTA.
The reason this government is bringing forward this enabling legislation, which is an act to support this agreement, is that we believe it is good for Canada. Interestingly, so does Canadian business. The people who create jobs in this country believe it will be good for Canada, and it will be good for Canada.
My hon. friend's third question made reference to parallel discussions with respect to the environment and labour. I want to assure my hon. friend that the government thinks it is a marvellous idea to proceed with further negotiations with respect to the environment and labour issues.
A year ago, in March 1992, we proposed to our two partners in this agreement that we should do a parallel agreement with respect to the environment. The American government of the day was not interested. Now we,
March 15, 1993

have a government in the United States that is interested and of course Canada fully supports it.
As the American president himself has made abundantly clear, the NAFTA will not be reopened for negotiation. That agreement was negotiated over many months by the three parties and will not be reopened. Hopefully we will reach an accord with respect to the environment. Even so, I want my hon. friends to be aware of the fact that never in the history of the world has there been a trade agreement concluded with as many provisions on the environment as the NAFTA.
In conclusion, I want them to be aware of the fact that the NAFTA contains a strong commitment to the concept of sustainable development and environmental protection. I want them to bear in mind that what is most important to Canadians is the protection of our own environment. Nothing in the NAFTA precludes our ability to establish our own environmental standards.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the member for South Shore. What we have experienced in this member's speech today is the typical Conservative lean, mean machine approach in the name of global competitiveness.
I realize that in every trade deal there are winners and there are losers. The problem we have today is that a lot of people are losing. A lot of people are unemployed, almost a couple of million.
I was reading an article on the weekend written by Joe Mancini who was talking about competitive global mass production, more threat than promise. He made an interesting statement. He said: "Communities and families are dissolving as work takes on an increasing importance and puts greater demands on people's time. This trend in work results in spouses not having time to experience their children. People do not have time to build community outside work. The result is increasing isolation. Growth as recorded by Statistics Canada is no guarantee of economic development. Unfortunately politics is such that illusions of growth are more important than real innovation. Individuals and families can disentangle from these illusions by creating real growth through innovation in the household using traditional skills".

Mr. Speaker, I tried with care to listen to my hon. friend's question, although I must say he confused me a bit with his logic.
I noticed that he mentioned, for example, a couple of million unemployed in this country. I think he would admit that was a rather gross exaggeration. If an individual is unemployed, that is one too many. I am sure that is the way this government and all members of the House feel.
He talked about ratcheting down inflation as if it were a terrible thing. I am not sure I understand where he is coming from. What is inflation all about? Inflation is a killer. Inflation is the thing that says to people on fixed incomes like our seniors that next year they are not going to be able to pay for what they have.
By getting inflation under control and having price stability we provide the best basis for people to be able to plan their lives and to live in some comfort and with some harmony. I do not understand why my friend would take issue with that approach.
I think his question was also about the issue of globalization and whether or not Canada should respond to what is happening in the world. I do not understand where he is coming from. It seems to me we have Canadians telling us by their actions that we have to smarten up and sort out what is happening in the world.
When Canadians prefer to shop in other countries they are telling us that we are not competitive, even in our own markets. When we have Canadians saying they want to see growth and job opportunities we know we have to go beyond our own market as we have in the past. We have to be able to export.
Other countries of the world are catching up in terms of productivity and technology whether or not my hon. friend wants to acknowledge it. The bottom line is that the responsibility of the government is to Canadians. It must prepare the Canadian economy so we are in the best position, for the benefit of Canadians, to have

Mr. Speaker, at this point, our party would like to divide the following half hour into speeches of ten minutes each.

The issue before us because of this NDP resolution is in part the abrogation of the free trade agreement and the non-signing of the NAFTA. My friend from South Shore has lauded the positive benefits he says we have seen from free trade, but it is impossible to separate actual results under free trade from what occurred in the economy as a whole. Let us be intellectually honest.
If we look at the record over the past four years since free trade came in we find our unemployment is now at
10.8	per cent. In the United States it is at 7 per cent. Our manufacturing job losses in those four years now stand at 16 per cent. In the United States it has only been 6 per cent. Why have we been devastated so much more than the United States during that period of time?
We can look at an even more alarming statistic. Our ability to compete has been declining. We are now growing at about half the rate of that of our major competitors in the G-7. This is alarming in terms of our future ability to create the wealth we need in this country to sustain the high level of humane social programs which are a hallmark of the Canadian way of life.
Perhaps even more alarming when we look at the Tory record is that in 1984 Canada had a high-tech trade surplus of $1 billion. Today that high-tech trade surplus has become a deficit of $30 billion. Even though trade may have picked up a bit with the United States in recent years, we are losing in spades when it comes to the high-tech, value-added industries which will create the high paying jobs of the future we need if we are to compete with low $1.50 an hour Mexican labour.
What are the lessons we can take from our four years under free trade? My conclusion is that trade is not the real issue. Trade agreements such as the free trade agreement and the NAFTA are not the overriding economic issue we face. Even if we got rid of free trade we would still find ourselves having to compete as a
trading nation. As one whose GDP is 30 per cent more than even Japan's we are dependent on foreign trade. We still need ways in which to compete.
Perhaps we can learn from our four years under free trade. I would like to focus on seven lessons that we should have learned.
First, Canada can no longer depend on its abundant natural resources and the effortless economic superiority those have given us to sustain our high standard of living. We need the value-added, high-wage jobs.
Second, if we are going to enter into another free trade agreement surely we have learned that we need detailed impact assessments so that we can predict where the job losses are going to occur, as they inevitably will. We need adjustment programs to make sure that those workers who are affected adversely have jobs and are not doomed to perpetual unemployment.
The NDP would have us abolish these trade agreements or not enter into them. However, in its resolution, has it called for the adjustment programs that we need? Of course, it has not. It has totally overlooked it. Has it, in asking us to totally abolish these trade agreements, given us an impact analysis of how many job losses would occur because our access to foreign markets could be diminished? It has not taken that responsible step of forewarning us as to the consequences of its policy.
The third lesson I hope we have learned is that even though we have a free trade agreement, this does not guarantee secure access to the foreign market. We have learned that tariffs were not the real barrier. Issues such as anti-dumping, countervail and government procurement have been far greater barriers to Canadian access to the U.S. market.
The fourth lesson is that the unparalleled level of trade harassment by the Americans against Canadian producers is not ended. We are not going to have the so-called benefits that the member for South Shore talked about. These are the benefits of investment. No firm is going to invest in Canada be it a Canadian or a foreign firm. They will just not put their new money here to service the North American market if this unmitigated trade harassment can continue. Our producers can have the threat of being shut out of the American market through spurious actions such as we have seen with
March 15, 1993

respect to Honda, softwood, pork and now steel in a major way.
Has the government given us any hope that under the NAFTA it has found a way to end that trade harassment? As a matter of fact, no, it will not even talk about bringing in a subsidies code to deal with countervailing let alone some new measures and common laws to deal with the question of anti-dumping.
The fifth lesson I hope we have learned is that when we have a free trade agreement there is going to be an international rationalization of investment. We know this is inevitable. The problem is that this rationalization of industry has been mainly outside Canada. More than 50 per cent of our manufacturing sector is controlled by foreigners, mainly Americans. When there is a slight recession or an opportunity to consolidate plants, one is not going to consolidate the American operation and head office into the Canadian branch plant. The opposite occurs. This is going to be a structural problem that not only this government, but succeeding governments, are going to have to come to grips with.
Sixth, I hope we have learned that trade policy does not take place in an economic vacuum. It is one portion of our economic agenda but a very small one when looked at on the whole. For example, this government's high interest rate, high dollar and high tax policies over the past four years have done more to create barriers to Canadian producers than the removal of all the tariffs that have taken place under the free trade agreement. When the dollar goes up 27 per cent from a low to a high of 90 cents, that jump is a far greater barrier than any of the trade tariffs that were abolished.
Finally, the seventh lesson is for us to recognize that trade policy is only one aspect of an industrial policy. What we need is a comprehensive industrial policy that will deal with our ability to compete. We need to integrate fiscal and monetary policies so they work for Canadian producers. We need to get rid of the high levels of illiteracy and innumeracy that make our workers unfit for the plant. We must deal with the 38 per cent drop-out rate in high schools. We must deal with our

declining level of research and development that is less than half that of our competitors and is falling. We must deal with the Mexican challenge. Mexico now produces four times the number of scientists and engineers that Canada does.
If we are going to compete, then these are the real issues and this is why we need a comprehensive industrial policy. This is why trade is not the real issue. This is why the NDP has so far missed the mark in this resolution. There is no way that any intellectually honest or right-thinking person could ever support it.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is just as free to renegotiate the free trade agreement as the NDP is to switch its policies.
Our position is very simple. We want to renegotiate this free trade agreement involving Mexico because we find it deficient. Unlike the government, we are not in favour of rushing in to pass this deal at a time when the United States has put it on hold. It is totally irresponsible.
